stimulus.title: Estimated Population of Early Cities (c. 2500 BCE)

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the table of Bronze Age cities?

options.text: Early large cities clustered along fertile river valleys
Memphis held more residents than Uruk and Mohenjo-daro combined
Mohenjo-daro developed along the Euphrates River delta
Urban populations shrank rapidly after irrigation began

explanation: All three Bronze Age cities—Uruk, Memphis, and Mohenjo-daro—grew along major river valleys.
fun_fact: Uruk's mud-brick city wall stretched nearly six miles around its temples and neighborhoods.

trap_notes.b: Memphis had 30,000 residents, far fewer than Uruk's 50,000 alone.
trap_notes.c: The table places Mohenjo-daro in the Indus basin, not the Euphrates.
trap_notes.d: The table shows large urban centers sustained by river agriculture, not shrinking cities.
trap_notes.default: Check the River Basin column: every city listed relied on a major river system.

stimulus.title: Roman Silver Denarius Purity Over Time

prompt: What fiscal trend does the Roman denarius silver table illustrate?

options.text: Emperors minted purer coins as borders expanded
The state debased silver coins to stretch war and state budgets
Roman merchants abandoned silver coins for barter by 68 CE
Nero raised silver purity above Augustus's standard

explanation: Silver content dropped from 95% to 75%, showing emperors stretched revenues by debasing coinage.
fun_fact: By the late third century CE, the denarius contained less than 5 percent silver.

trap_notes.a: The percentages fall from 95% to 75%, showing declining rather than rising purity.
trap_notes.c: Coins remained in circulation; the table measures coin purity, not a return to barter.
trap_notes.d: Nero's 90% purity was lower than Augustus's 95%.
trap_notes.default: Notice the steady drop in silver percentage from Augustus to Marcus Aurelius.

stimulus.title: Han China & Roman Empire Estimates (c. 150 CE)

prompt: Which statement accurately compares the Han and Roman empires in the table?

options.text: Han China had a larger population, while Rome built more roads
Rome held more than twice Han China's total population
Han China built more than twice as many roads as Rome
Together the two empires ruled under ten percent of humanity

explanation: Han China's 60 million exceeded Rome's 55 million, whereas Rome's 80,000 km of roads topped Han China's.
fun_fact: Both empires built courier relay stations along their roads to speed imperial dispatches.

trap_notes.b: Han China's estimated population of 60 million was slightly larger than Rome's 55 million.
trap_notes.c: Rome's 80,000 km road network was more than double Han China's 35,000 km.
trap_notes.d: The table lists their combined share at roughly 45 percent of world population.
trap_notes.default: Compare both columns carefully: Han leads in population, while Rome leads in road length.

prompt: What technological shift accompanied Song China's surge in iron production?

options.text: Iron output fell sharply as wood supplies grew
Switching from charcoal to coal and coke supported much higher output
Charcoal remained the sole fuel for furnaces in 1078 CE
Iron production stayed flat between 998 CE and 1078 CE

explanation: Moving from charcoal to coal and coke coincided with a jump to 125,000 tons by 1078 CE.
fun_fact: Song ironworkers used water-powered bellows to blast air into high-temperature furnaces.

trap_notes.a: Output rose nearly tenfold from 13,500 tons to 125,000 tons.
trap_notes.c: By 1078 CE, the table shows coal and coke as the primary fuel.
trap_notes.d: Output nearly quadrupled between 998 CE and 1078 CE.
trap_notes.default: Look at both the tonnage jump and the change in the Primary Fuel column.

prompt: How did the Black Death's population drop affect English farm wages?

options.text: Labor shortages pushed real wages higher for surviving workers
Falling population caused real wages to drop below 1300 levels
English population doubled immediately after 1350
Wages stayed frozen at 100 despite demographic loss

explanation: As population fell from 5.0 to 2.5 million, scarce workers commanded a 75% higher real wage index.
fun_fact: English landlords passed the 1351 Statute of Labourers to cap wages, sparking peasant unrest.

trap_notes.b: The Real Wage Index rose from 100 to 175, rather than falling.
trap_notes.c: Population was nearly cut in half, dropping from 5.0 million to 2.7 million.
trap_notes.d: The wage index climbed steadily in each period after 1347.
trap_notes.default: Compare the falling population column against the rising real wage index.

prompt: What does the voyage comparison table reveal about early Ming maritime capacity?

options.text: Columbus sailed earlier with a much larger fleet
Zheng He led far larger fleets before European voyages
Da Gama commanded more ships than Zheng He's fleet
Ming fleets sailed only in the 1490s alongside Spain

explanation: Zheng He's 1405 fleet of 317 ships sailed nearly 90 years before Columbus and da Gama's small squadrons.
fun_fact: Zheng He's seven voyages reached Hormuz, Aden, and East African ports like Malindi.

trap_notes.a: Zheng He sailed in 1405 with 317 ships; Columbus sailed in 1492 with 3 ships.
trap_notes.c: Da Gama commanded 4 ships, far fewer than Zheng He's 317.
trap_notes.d: Zheng He's voyages took place in the early 1400s, ending in 1433.
trap_notes.default: Check both the Year and Fleet Size columns to compare Ming and European expeditions.

stimulus.title: Estimated Indigenous Population of Central Mexico

prompt: Which historical development explains the catastrophic drop shown in the table?

options.text: Rapid industrialization drew villagers to distant cities
Voluntary migration to Europe emptied Central Mexico
Old World diseases, conquest, and forced labor devastated communities
Population recovered to half its 1518 total by 1605

explanation: Smallpox, measles, warfare, and forced labor reduced Central Mexico's Indigenous population by over 90%.
fun_fact: Because Indigenous Americans lacked prior immunity, virgin-soil epidemics struck repeatedly.

trap_notes.a: Industrialization did not occur in 16th-century Mexico.
trap_notes.b: Indigenous populations declined in place from disease and conquest, not European emigration.
trap_notes.d: By 1605, the table shows population had fallen to just 4 percent of the 1518 level.
trap_notes.default: A 96% drop between 1518 and 1605 reflects epidemic disease and colonial conquest.

stimulus.title: Transatlantic Slave Trade Arrivals by Region

prompt: What does the table show about the geographic distribution of the transatlantic slave trade?

options.text: British North America received the majority of enslaved Africans
Brazil and the Caribbean absorbed most enslaved people, largely for sugar
Tobacco plantations in Brazil drove the largest share of arrivals
Fewer than one million enslaved Africans crossed the Atlantic

explanation: Brazil (4.8M) and the Caribbean (4.0M) received the vast majority of enslaved Africans, mainly for sugar.
fun_fact: Brazil was the last country in the Western Hemisphere to abolish slavery, doing so in 1888.

trap_notes.a: British North America received about 0.4 million, a small share compared to Brazil and the Caribbean.
trap_notes.c: The table lists sugar and coffee for Brazil, and tobacco and cotton for North America.
trap_notes.d: The three regions alone total over 9 million arrivals.
trap_notes.default: Compare the Est. Arrivals column: Brazil and the Caribbean far outnumber North America.

prompt: Which conclusion follows from the global silver production table?

options.text: European mines produced more silver than the Americas
Japan mined more silver than Potosi and Zacatecas
Spanish American mines supplied most of the world's silver
China produced over half of global silver output

explanation: Spanish American mines at Potosi and Zacatecas supplied roughly 70% of world silver output.
fun_fact: Ming and Qing China required taxes in silver, pulling American and Japanese silver to East Asia.

trap_notes.a: Europe and other regions accounted for roughly 15%, compared to 70% in Spanish America.
trap_notes.b: Japan produced about 15%, far below Spanish America's 70%.
trap_notes.d: China was a major buyer of silver, not a top producer in the table.
trap_notes.default: Spanish America's ~70% share dominated early modern silver production.

prompt: How did Gutenberg's movable-type press affect European book output?

options.text: Book output multiplied over tenfold between 1451 and 1600
Printed book volume declined after 1500 as paper grew scarce
Scribes hand-copied most of the 137 million books in 1551–1600
Printing spread only within Mainz before 1600

explanation: Output surged from 12.5 million copies in 1451–1500 to 137 million in 1551–1600 via movable type.
fun_fact: Cheap printed pamphlets let Renaissance scholars and Reformation preachers reach wide audiences.

trap_notes.b: Output rose sharply in every half-century listed.
trap_notes.c: The table identifies the movable-type press as the primary format.
trap_notes.d: Producing 137 million copies reflected presses operating across Europe.
trap_notes.default: Compare 12.5 million in 1451–1500 to 137 million a century later.

prompt: What does the surge in British cotton imports from 1760 to 1840 demonstrate?

options.text: Britain grew enough domestic cotton to end foreign imports
Mechanized mills drove a massive expansion in global cotton demand
Cotton imports peaked in 1760 before steam power arrived
Manchester's textile factories closed down by 1840

explanation: Imports jumped from 2.5 to 592 million pounds as steam-powered Lancashire mills scaled up production.
fun_fact: Much of Manchester's raw cotton after 1800 came from enslaved-labor plantations in the U.S. South.

trap_notes.a: Britain's cool climate cannot grow cotton; all raw cotton was imported.
trap_notes.c: Imports were smallest in 1760 and over 200 times larger by 1840.
trap_notes.d: The huge 1840 import figure reflects booming factory demand in Manchester.
trap_notes.default: Look at the jump from 2.5 million lbs in 1760 to 592 million lbs in 1840.

prompt: Which trend appears in the European railroad expansion table?

options.text: Britain still held the longest rail network in 1890
Russia built no railroads until after 1890
Germany overtook Britain in total rail track by 1890
Rail construction slowed across all three countries after 1850

explanation: Germany expanded from 5,856 km in 1850 to 42,869 km in 1890, surpassing Great Britain's 27,827 km.
fun_fact: Railroads helped Prussia mobilize troops rapidly during the wars of German unification.

trap_notes.a: In 1890, both Germany (42,869 km) and Russia (30,596 km) exceeded Britain's track length.
trap_notes.b: Russia had 501 km in 1850 and expanded to 30,596 km by 1890.
trap_notes.d: All three countries multiplied their track length between 1850 and 1890.
trap_notes.default: Compare the 1890 column across all three countries.

prompt: What global economic shift from 1750 to 1900 is shown in the table?

options.text: China and India remained the top manufacturers in 1900
Europe industrialized while Asia's manufacturing share dropped sharply
Europe produced over 60% of world goods in 1750
India's manufacturing share doubled between 1750 and 1900

explanation: Europe's share rose from 23.2% to 62.0% via industrialization, while China and India fell sharply.
fun_fact: Cheap British machine-woven cloth undercut handloom weavers across colonial India.

trap_notes.a: By 1900, China (6.2%) and India (1.7%) trailed far behind Europe (62.0%).
trap_notes.c: Europe's 1750 share was 23.2%, smaller than China's 32.8%.
trap_notes.d: India's share fell from 24.5% to 1.7%.
trap_notes.default: Compare 1750 and 1900: Asia led in 1750, but Europe dominated by 1900.

prompt: Which pair of factors caused the demographic drop shown in Ireland's census data?

options.text: Potato blight famine deaths and mass overseas emigration
Industrialization and a sharp rise in urban birth rates
World War I mobilization and border redrawing
Rapid population recovery between 1851 and 1861

explanation: The 1845–1852 Great Famine killed roughly one million people and drove over a million to emigrate.
fun_fact: Ireland's population has still not returned to its pre-famine 1841 peak of over eight million.

trap_notes.b: Higher birth rates would increase population, not reduce it by 29 percent.
trap_notes.c: World War I began in 1914, decades after the 1841–1861 censuses.
trap_notes.d: Population kept falling from 6.55 million in 1851 to 5.80 million in 1861.
trap_notes.default: A 20% drop by 1851 reflects the Irish Potato Famine and mass emigration.

prompt: What does the table indicate about Japan during the Meiji era?

options.text: Japan rejected railroads to preserve samurai domains
Japan rapidly built modern transport, energy, and export industries
Coal mining declined as Japan stayed purely agricultural
Silk exports ended once coal production grew

explanation: Meiji reforms expanded rail from 61 to 7,690 km and coal nearly twentyfold while leading silk exports.
fun_fact: Foreign currency earned from silk exports helped Meiji Japan buy industrial machinery abroad.

trap_notes.a: Meiji Japan abolished samurai domains and expanded rail to 7,690 km by 1905.
trap_notes.c: Coal output jumped from 600,000 to 11.6 million tons.
trap_notes.d: Japan became the world's leading raw silk exporter by 1905.
trap_notes.default: Every indicator in the table shows rapid industrial and export growth.

prompt: Which statement is supported by the Scramble for Africa table?

options.text: Europeans already ruled most of Africa in 1870
Europe partitioned nearly all of Africa by 1914
African states regained full independence by 1914
Only coastal ports fell under European control

explanation: European control surged from roughly 10% in 1870 to 90% in 1914, leaving only Ethiopia and Liberia free.
fun_fact: Ethiopia defeated Italy at the 1896 Battle of Adwa to preserve its independence.

trap_notes.a: In 1870, Europeans controlled only about 10 percent of Africa.
trap_notes.c: Decolonization occurred after World War II, not before 1914.
trap_notes.d: Control rose to 90% of the continent, far beyond coastal ports.
trap_notes.default: Compare 1870 (~10%) to 1914 (~90%) under European rule.

stimulus.title: World War I Military Mobilization & Deaths

prompt: What does the table reveal about the scale of World War I?

options.text: Industrial warfare caused millions of military deaths across major powers
France mobilized more soldiers than Russia and Germany
Russia suffered higher military deaths than Germany
Total military deaths across the three powers stayed under one million

explanation: Each of the three powers mobilized over 8 million troops and lost well over a million soldiers.
fun_fact: Machine guns, heavy artillery, and poison gas made World War I's Western Front deeply lethal.

trap_notes.b: France mobilized 8.4 million, fewer than Russia (12M) and Germany (11M).
trap_notes.c: Germany's ~2.0 million military deaths exceeded Russia's ~1.8 million.
trap_notes.d: Combined military deaths for these three nations alone exceeded 5 million.
trap_notes.default: All three nations mobilized millions of troops and suffered over a million deaths each.

stimulus.title: Price of a Loaf of Bread in Berlin

prompt: How did Weimar Germany's 1923 hyperinflation affect everyday life?

options.text: Rapid money-printing made the mark nearly worthless, wiping out savings
Bread prices fell steadily after the Ruhr occupation began
The German mark gained purchasing power against food in 1923
Prices returned to 1918 levels by November 1923

explanation: Printing paper marks to pay striking Ruhr workers drove bread from 250 marks to 200 billion marks.
fun_fact: Workers were sometimes paid twice a day so they could buy food before prices rose again.

trap_notes.b: Bread jumped from 250 marks in January to 200 billion marks in November 1923.
trap_notes.c: Needing 200 billion marks for one loaf shows a collapse in purchasing power.
trap_notes.d: November 1923 marked the peak of hyperinflation, not a return to 1918 prices.
trap_notes.default: A loaf jumping from 0.63 to 200 billion marks shows extreme currency collapse.

prompt: What priority of Stalin's Five-Year Plans is reflected in the table?

options.text: Shifting resources away from heavy industry toward consumer goods
Rapid state-directed growth in coal, steel, and electric power
Closing state factories to restore small private farms
Reducing electricity output to conserve coal

explanation: Stalin's first two Five-Year Plans multiplied heavy industrial output in coal, steel, and electricity.
fun_fact: While heavy industry surged, collectivization and grain seizures caused devastating famine in 1932–1933.

trap_notes.a: The table measures heavy industry—coal, steel, and electricity—not consumer goods.
trap_notes.c: Stalin abolished private farms through forced collectivization.
trap_notes.d: Electricity output rose more than sevenfold between 1928 and 1937.
trap_notes.default: Coal, steel, and electricity all tripled or quadrupled under the Five-Year Plans.

prompt: What happened to global trade during the first four years of the Great Depression?

options.text: World trade value fell by roughly two-thirds amid rising tariffs
Tariff cuts kept world imports steady at 100
Global imports rose sharply between 1931 and 1933
Currency devaluations doubled world trade by 1933

explanation: Retaliatory tariffs and collapsing demand cut the world imports index from 100 in 1929 to 35 in 1933.
fun_fact: Economist Charles Kindleberger famously graphed this downward spiral as the 'contraction spiral' of trade.

trap_notes.b: Countries raised tariffs rather than cutting them, and imports fell from 100 to 35.
trap_notes.c: The index fell from 60 in 1931 to 35 in 1933.
trap_notes.d: World trade shrank by 65 percent rather than doubling.
trap_notes.default: Follow the index from 100 in 1929 down to 35 in 1933.

prompt: How did industrial output shape the Allied victory shown in the table?

options.text: Germany outproduced the United States and Soviet Union combined
Allied aircraft production far outstripped German output by 1944
Soviet aircraft production fell after 1941
U.S. factories built fewer planes in 1944 than in 1941

explanation: In 1944, the U.S. (96,318) and USSR (40,300) together built over three times as many planes as Germany.
fun_fact: The Soviet Union dismantled entire factories ahead of the 1941 German invasion and rebuilt them east of the Urals.

trap_notes.a: Germany built 39,807 planes in 1944, less than half of U.S. output alone.
trap_notes.c: Soviet output more than doubled from 15,735 in 1941 to 40,300 in 1944.
trap_notes.d: U.S. output more than tripled between 1941 and 1944.
trap_notes.default: Add the 1944 Allied figures (96,318 + 40,300) and compare with Germany's 39,807.

prompt: What does the table show about the immediate human cost of the 1947 Partition?

options.text: Borderlines divided Punjab and Bengal with minimal movement
Partition triggered one of history's largest mass migrations and deadly violence
British India stayed united as a single federation after 1947
Refugee movements were limited to southern coastal ports

explanation: Drawing borders across Punjab and Bengal displaced 14–15 million people and killed 1–2 million.
fun_fact: British lawyer Cyril Radcliffe drew the Partition boundary lines in just five weeks without ever visiting India.

trap_notes.a: Roughly 14 to 15 million people were displaced across the new borders.
trap_notes.c: British India split into two independent states, India and Pakistan.
trap_notes.d: The table identifies Punjab and Bengal as the primary regions affected.
trap_notes.default: Look at the displaced population (14–15 million) and death toll (1–2 million).

prompt: What outcome followed Marshall Plan aid in Western Europe?

options.text: Western European industrial output surpassed prewar 1938 levels
West Germany received more Marshall Plan aid than Britain
French industry remained below 1938 output in 1951
Marshall Plan funds went exclusively to Eastern Europe

explanation: All three major recipients boosted industrial output 30% to 40% above prewar 1938 levels by 1951.
fun_fact: The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid and barred Eastern European satellites from participating.

trap_notes.b: Britain received $3.3B, more than double West Germany's $1.4B.
trap_notes.c: France's industrial output rose 40% above its 1938 level.
trap_notes.d: All three recipients listed were in Western Europe.
trap_notes.default: Check the Industrial Output Change column: every recipient exceeded 1938 levels.

stimulus.title: African Nations Gaining Independence by Decade

prompt: Which decade marked the peak wave of African decolonization in the table?

options.text: The 1950s, when 32 African states won independence
The 1960s, when 32 African nations became independent
The 1970s, when Ghana became the first free colony
The 1980s, when Nigeria gained independence

explanation: Thirty-two African nations achieved independence in the 1960s, including 17 in 1960 alone.
fun_fact: 1960 is often called the 'Year of Africa' because 17 African nations gained independence that year.

trap_notes.a: Only 6 nations gained independence in the 1950s; 32 did so in the 1960s.
trap_notes.c: Ghana gained independence in 1957, during the 1950s.
trap_notes.d: Nigeria gained independence in 1960, as shown in the 1960s row.
trap_notes.default: Compare the middle column: 32 states in the 1960s far exceeds 6 or 9.

prompt: What impact of the Green Revolution does the Indian wheat table show?

options.text: Wheat output tripled using high-yield inputs
Dwarf wheat varieties cut harvests in half
Traditional seeds outproduced dwarf wheat
Indian wheat production stalled after 1970

explanation: High-yield seeds, irrigation, and chemical fertilizers helped triple India's wheat harvest by 1980.
fun_fact: Agronomist Norman Borlaug won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize for developing disease-resistant dwarf wheat.

trap_notes.b: Output doubled by 1970 and tripled by 1980.
trap_notes.c: Output was lowest (10.3 million tons) when traditional seeds were used.
trap_notes.d: Production rose from 20.1 million tons in 1970 to 31.8 million tons in 1980.
trap_notes.default: Wheat output grew from 10.3 to 31.8 million tons with Green Revolution inputs.

stimulus.title: South Korea Real GDP per Capita (1960–1990)

prompt: Which development strategy does South Korea's table illustrate?

options.text: Export-led industrialization climbing from textiles to electronics
Closing ports to foreign trade to focus on subsistence farming
Falling income per person between 1975 and 1990
Relying solely on raw material exports through 1990

explanation: South Korea shifted from raw materials to textiles, ships, and electronics, multiplying GDP per capita.
fun_fact: South Korea became one of the 'Four Asian Tigers' alongside Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Singapore.

trap_notes.b: South Korea's growth relied on export-oriented manufacturing, not autarky.
trap_notes.c: GDP per capita jumped more than tenfold between 1975 and 1990.
trap_notes.d: By 1990, electronics and autos led exports.
trap_notes.default: Notice both the steep GDP rise and the shift toward higher-tech exports.

prompt: What social trend accompanied China's market reforms from 1981 to 2005?

options.text: Urbanization more than doubled while extreme poverty fell sharply
Extreme poverty rose above 80% as cities expanded
China's rural population share grew between 1981 and 2005
Poverty rates stayed unchanged despite factory growth

explanation: China's urban share rose from 20% to 43% as extreme poverty plunged from 88% to 19%.
fun_fact: Hundreds of millions of rural workers migrated to coastal factory cities during this boom.

trap_notes.b: Extreme poverty dropped from 88% in 1981 to 19% in 2005.
trap_notes.c: Since the urban share rose from 20% to 43%, the rural share declined.
trap_notes.d: Poverty fell by nearly 70 percentage points over 24 years.
trap_notes.default: Compare the rising Urban Share column with the falling Extreme Poverty Rate column.

stimulus.title: Average Crude Oil Price per Barrel

prompt: What does the oil price table show about the 1970s energy crises?

options.text: Middle East geopolitical shocks drove oil prices up more than tenfold
Oil prices dropped below $3 per barrel after the 1973 embargo
The Iranian Revolution cut crude prices in half in 1980
OPEC lost all influence over world oil prices after 1972

explanation: Oil jumped from $2.48 in 1972 to $11.58 after the 1973–1974 embargo and $36.83 during Iran's revolution.
fun_fact: The 1973 embargo prompted Western nations to create the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and fuel-economy standards.

trap_notes.b: Oil rose from $2.48 to $11.58 after the embargo.
trap_notes.c: Prices more than tripled between 1974 ($11.58) and 1980 ($36.83).
trap_notes.d: The 1973–1974 embargo demonstrated OPEC members' leverage over global energy.
trap_notes.default: Track the barrel price from $2.48 in 1972 to $36.83 in 1980.

prompt: Which trend is shown in the Cold War nuclear stockpile table?

options.text: Superpowers built huge arsenals before treaty cuts
The USSR held more warheads than the U.S. in 1965
Both arsenals grew larger between 1985 and 2000
Nuclear disarmament was finished by the year 2000

explanation: Stockpiles peaked in the tens of thousands during the Cold War, then fell sharply by 2000 under START treaties.
fun_fact: The 1987 INF Treaty was the first pact to eliminate an entire class of nuclear missiles.

trap_notes.b: In 1965, the U.S. held 31,139 warheads compared to the USSR's 6,129.
trap_notes.c: Both countries cut their arsenals by more than half between 1985 and 2000.
trap_notes.d: Over 22,000 warheads remained combined in 2000.
trap_notes.default: Notice the buildup to 1985 followed by steep reductions by 2000.

prompt: What does the table show about global human health in the late 20th century?

options.text: Public health gains added 20 years to life expectancy
Global life expectancy fell after smallpox ended
Average life expectancy stayed under 50 in 2000
Antibiotics had no measurable effect after 1950

explanation: Global average life expectancy climbed from 46.5 years in 1950 to 66.5 years in 2000.
fun_fact: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980—the first human disease wiped out.

trap_notes.b: Life expectancy rose from 59.4 years in 1975 to 66.5 years in 2000.
trap_notes.c: By 2000, the global average reached 66.5 years.
trap_notes.d: The largest jump—nearly 13 years—occurred between 1950 and 1975.
trap_notes.default: Compare 46.5 years in 1950 with 66.5 years in 2000.

prompt: How did Indian Ocean monsoon winds shape cultural exchange between East Africa and India?

options.text: Predictable wind reversals kept sailors in ports for months, fostering diasporas
Year-round hurricanes blocked all direct sea voyages across the Arabian Sea
Monsoons blew only southward, forcing merchants to walk back overland
Frozen winter harbors closed East African ports for half of each year

explanation: Seasonal monsoon reversals gave sailors predictable round trips and months in port to marry and trade.
fun_fact: Swahili language and coastal Islam grew out of centuries of Indian Ocean maritime contact.

trap_notes.b: Dhows sailed reliably across the Arabian Sea for centuries using monsoon schedules.
trap_notes.c: Monsoons reverse direction seasonally, blowing southwest in summer and northeast in winter.
trap_notes.d: East African tropical ports never freeze.
trap_notes.default: Seasonal wind reversals created predictable round-trip voyages and long port layovers.

prompt: Why did Song and Yuan paper money and credit bills expand long-distance Eurasian trade?

options.text: They lowered transaction costs by replacing heavy metal coin shipments
They banned silver and silk from crossing Mongol borders
They eliminated all caravan taxes along Silk Road oases
They forced European banks to adopt Chinese characters

explanation: Paper notes and flying-cash credit bills let merchants settle large trades without hauling heavy coins.
fun_fact: Marco Polo marveled that Kublai Khan's mulberry-bark notes worked as currency across the empire.

trap_notes.b: Silver and silk remained prized trade goods across Eurasia.
trap_notes.c: States still collected customs duties at oasis gates and ports.
trap_notes.d: European merchants used their own bills of exchange and Latin scripts.
trap_notes.default: Paper credit reduced the weight, risk, and cost of moving metal coins.

prompt: How does classical Athenian democracy differ from modern representative republics?

options.text: Athenian citizens voted directly on laws, whereas modern republics elect lawmakers
Athens granted full voting rights to women and enslaved residents
Modern republics select officials by random lottery like Athens's council
Athenian assemblies met only once every four years to pick a king

explanation: Athens practiced direct democracy by male citizens in the Assembly, whereas modern republics use elected representatives.
fun_fact: Athens also used sortition—random lottery—to choose most magistrates and jurors.

trap_notes.b: Women, foreigners, and enslaved people were excluded from Athenian citizenship.
trap_notes.c: Modern republics rely on elections rather than random lottery for legislatures.
trap_notes.d: The Athenian Assembly met dozens of times a year and had no king.
trap_notes.default: Direct citizen voting in Athens contrasts with elected legislatures today.

prompt: How did the Inca state overcome steep Andean mountain climates to supply its population?

options.text: It linked different altitude zones by stone roads and state storehouses
It imported wheat by ocean galleons from Europe
It abandoned highland farms to settle only Amazonian lowlands
It relied on camel caravans crossing the Atacama Desert

explanation: Inca ayllus farmed terraced altitude zones and moved potatoes, maize, and wool via state roads and qullqa storehouses.
fun_fact: Freeze-dried potatoes called chuno could be stored in Inca warehouses for years against famine.

trap_notes.b: The Inca Empire had no pre-1532 contact with European wheat or galleons.
trap_notes.c: Highland valleys around Cusco and Lake Titicaca remained the Inca demographic core.
trap_notes.d: Llamas and alpacas, not camels, carried goods in the Andes.
trap_notes.default: Connecting multiple elevation zones let the Incas exchange crops across climates.

prompt: How did massive American silver imports affect Europe's 16th-century economy?

options.text: Expanding the money supply without matching goods caused sustained inflation
Silver abundance pushed grain and bread prices steadily downward
Spain used silver to avoid all European wars and debts
Silver imports ended European demand for Asian spices and silk

explanation: Floods of silver coin outpaced agricultural and craft output, driving Europe's 'Price Revolution.'
fun_fact: Despite Potosi's wealth, Spain defaulted on royal debts multiple times due to costly European wars.

trap_notes.b: More money chasing limited goods pushed prices upward, not downward.
trap_notes.c: Spain spent silver heavily on wars in the Netherlands, France, and the Mediterranean.
trap_notes.d: Europeans used American silver to buy even more Asian silk, tea, and spices.
trap_notes.default: Rapidly growing money supply relative to goods produces inflation.

prompt: Which Enlightenment principle links Locke's Two Treatises, the U.S. Declaration, and France's 1789 Declaration?

options.text: Legitimate government rests on consent and protects natural rights
Hereditary monarchs hold divine authority above written law
Mercantilist guilds should control all colonial trade
Established state churches must approve every elected official

explanation: All three texts argue that citizens possess natural rights and form governments by consent.
fun_fact: Thomas Jefferson and the Marquis de Lafayette consulted directly while drafting France's 1789 Declaration.

trap_notes.b: Enlightenment thinkers challenged divine-right absolutism.
trap_notes.c: Mercantilist guild monopolies were criticized by Enlightenment economists.
trap_notes.d: Enlightenment declarations moved toward religious toleration and secular rights.
trap_notes.default: Locke, Jefferson, and French revolutionaries all grounded rule in natural rights and consent.

prompt: Which geographic advantage helped Great Britain industrialize first?

options.text: Accessible coal and iron deposits near navigable rivers and ports
Vast domestic cotton fields along the Thames Valley
Landlocked borders that blocked foreign maritime competition
Tropical monsoon winds powering year-round hydro dams

explanation: Britain's shallow coal seams, iron ore, and short river-to-port distances lowered factory fuel and shipping costs.
fun_fact: Canals cut the cost of hauling coal to Manchester factories in half before railroads arrived.

trap_notes.b: Britain imported all of its raw cotton from the Americas, Egypt, and India.
trap_notes.c: Britain is an island nation with deep-water ports, not landlocked.
trap_notes.d: Monsoon winds belong to the Indian Ocean, not northern Europe.
trap_notes.default: Cheap coal, iron, and coastal waterways gave Britain a decisive early edge.

prompt: How did the Haitian Revolution directly reshape United States territorial expansion?

options.text: Haitian victory led Napoleon to sell Louisiana
Haiti annexed Florida and ceded it to Spain in 1804
French troops used Haiti as a base to retake Quebec
The United States ended all cotton farming in 1804

explanation: Losing Saint-Domingue ruined Napoleon's Caribbean empire plan, prompting the 1803 Louisiana Purchase.
fun_fact: Louisiana had been meant to supply food to Saint-Domingue's sugar plantations.

trap_notes.b: Spain held Florida until ceding it to the United States in 1819.
trap_notes.c: France lost its army to Haitian forces and yellow fever, abandoning North American plans.
trap_notes.d: U.S. cotton production expanded rapidly after 1803.
trap_notes.default: Without sugar-rich Saint-Domingue, Napoleon had little use for French Louisiana.

prompt: Why did British merchants export Indian opium to Qing China in the early 1800s?

options.text: To offset Britain's silver deficit from buying Chinese tea
To obey Qing laws banning silver imports into Guangzhou
To replace British wool factories with Chinese opium mills
To help Qing emperors fund repairs on the Grand Canal

explanation: High British demand for tea drained silver to China until Indian opium sales reversed the silver flow.
fun_fact: When Commissioner Lin Zexu banned opium in 1839, Britain launched the First Opium War.

trap_notes.b: Qing emperors welcomed silver and repeatedly outlawed opium imports.
trap_notes.c: Opium was an agricultural drug grown in India, not a factory product.
trap_notes.d: Opium smuggling drained silver out of Qing China, hurting imperial finances.
trap_notes.default: Britain used Indian opium to pay for Chinese tea without shipping silver.

prompt: Why did liberal nationalism threaten the multiethnic Austrian Empire in 1848?

options.text: Popular sovereignty and national self-rule challenged dynastic imperial rule
Nationalists demanded that Austria annex France and Spain
Liberals sought to restore feudal serfdom across Central Europe
Hungarian and Czech leaders wanted one German-speaking republic

explanation: Constitutions and national self-determination threatened to break apart the Habsburg multiethnic empire.
fun_fact: Although the 1848 revolutions were crushed, Austria finally abolished serfdom that year.

trap_notes.b: Nationalists wanted self-rule for their own peoples, not Habsburg expansion.
trap_notes.c: Liberals pushed to end feudal dues and gain written constitutions.
trap_notes.d: Czechs, Hungarians, and Italians sought autonomy from Vienna, not Germanization.
trap_notes.default: A multiethnic empire cannot easily survive demands for ethnic nation-states.

prompt: How did the 1869 Suez Canal transform trade and imperial strategy?

options.text: It bypassed southern Africa, making Egypt a vital chokepoint for Britain's route to India
It connected the Atlantic and Pacific oceans across Central America
It ended steamship use by favoring wooden sailing clippers
It isolated Mediterranean ports from Indian Ocean commerce

explanation: Cutting the sea route to India by thousands of miles made control of Egypt central to British strategy.
fun_fact: Sailing ships struggled with Red Sea winds, so the Suez Canal accelerated the shift to steamships.

trap_notes.b: That was the Panama Canal, opened in 1914.
trap_notes.c: The Suez Canal favored coal-fired steamships over sailing vessels.
trap_notes.d: The canal directly linked the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and Indian Ocean.
trap_notes.default: Shortening the London-to-Bombay voyage made Egypt a key imperial chokepoint.

prompt: How did the U.S. Civil War Union blockade reshape agriculture in Egypt and India?

options.text: Cutting Southern cotton exports sparked a cotton boom in Egypt and India
European textile mills switched from cotton to Andean wool
Egypt banned cotton farming to focus on wheat exports to Alabama
British mills stopped importing cotton until 1890

explanation: When the Union blockaded Confederate ports, British mills turned to Egypt and western India for raw cotton.
fun_fact: Egypt's cotton boom funded rail and canal projects before post-1865 price drops worsened its debt.

trap_notes.b: Lancashire mills stayed focused on cotton, seeking new suppliers abroad.
trap_notes.c: Egyptian landlords expanded cotton acreage rapidly during the 1861–1865 boom.
trap_notes.d: British mills sought alternative cotton supplies immediately during the 'Cotton Famine.'
trap_notes.default: Lost Confederate cotton drove European buyers to expand production in Egypt and India.

prompt: How did the 1884–1885 Berlin Conference borders affect postcolonial African states?

options.text: Arbitrary lines split ethnic groups and grouped rivals inside single states
African kingdoms drew borders along precolonial language boundaries
The conference guaranteed immediate self-rule for every colony
European powers banned all resource extraction across Central Africa

explanation: Colonial boundaries ignored African linguistic and political communities, creating lasting governance challenges.
fun_fact: Over 40 percent of modern African national borders follow straight geometric lines or rivers.

trap_notes.b: No African leaders attended the Berlin Conference.
trap_notes.c: The conference set rules for European occupation, not independence.
trap_notes.d: European powers raced to extract rubber, ivory, and minerals.
trap_notes.default: Geometric colonial borders often cut across existing African communities.

subdomain: Treaty of Versailles & League of Nations
prompt: Why did the League of Nations struggle to deter aggression in the 1930s?

options.text: It lacked a standing army, and major powers like the U.S. stayed outside it
The United States commanded League troops in every European crisis
The League outlawed all diplomatic treaties between democracies
Germany and Japan held permanent vetoes from 1919 onward

explanation: Without U.S. membership or enforcement forces, the League could not stop Japan, Italy, or Germany.
fun_fact: Although President Woodrow Wilson proposed the League, the U.S. Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles.

trap_notes.b: The United States never joined the League of Nations.
trap_notes.c: The League aimed to encourage open diplomacy, not ban treaties.
trap_notes.d: Germany joined only in 1926 and quit in 1933, the same year Japan withdrew.
trap_notes.default: Missing major powers and lacking military enforcement weakened the League.

prompt: What global problem were the 1944 Bretton Woods institutions designed to prevent?

options.text: 1930s-style currency devaluations and trade wars
The rapid spread of railroads across Western Europe
United Nations peacekeeping in decolonizing states
Gold mining across South Africa and Australia

explanation: The IMF and World Bank stabilized exchange rates and reconstruction loans to avoid 1930s-style economic collapse.
fun_fact: Bretton Woods pegged major currencies to the U.S. dollar, which was convertible to gold at $35 per ounce.

trap_notes.b: Railroads had been built a century earlier and were not the target.
trap_notes.c: UN peacekeeping was separate from the IMF and World Bank's monetary role.
trap_notes.d: The system anchored currencies to gold rather than banning gold mining.
trap_notes.default: Allied planners wanted stable currencies and open trade after the 1930s Depression.

prompt: How did the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights break new legal ground?

options.text: It set global standards for how states treat citizens
It built a single world parliament above national courts
It limited human rights protections to European kings
It abolished all sovereign national borders in 1948

explanation: Following WWII and the Holocaust, the UN declaration affirmed universal rights beyond state sovereignty.
fun_fact: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the UN drafting committee alongside delegates from Lebanon, China, and Chile.

trap_notes.b: The UN General Assembly adopted it as a declaration, not a world parliament.
trap_notes.c: Its 30 articles applied to all people globally regardless of region or status.
trap_notes.d: National borders and sovereign states remained intact.
trap_notes.default: After WWII atrocities, the UN set international human rights norms for all nations.

prompt: What did the 1956 Suez Crisis reveal about global power after World War II?

options.text: Britain and France needed U.S. backing to act abroad
Egypt lost sovereignty over the Nile River to France
The Soviet Union joined Britain to occupy Cairo
European empires regained control of Middle East oil

explanation: U.S. financial pressure forced Britain and France to withdraw, confirming Nasser's standing and superpower dominance.
fun_fact: The UN deployed its first armed peacekeeping force, UNEF, to monitor the Sinai withdrawal.

trap_notes.b: Egypt kept control of the Suez Canal after British, French, and Israeli troops withdrew.
trap_notes.c: The USSR threatened Britain and France and backed Egypt.
trap_notes.d: The crisis accelerated the decline of British and French influence in the Middle East.
trap_notes.default: Washington's pressure forced London and Paris to retreat from Egypt.

prompt: What diplomatic mechanism helped the U.S. and USSR resolve the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis?

options.text: A U.S. non-invasion pledge paired with Turkish missile removal
A full-scale NATO amphibious invasion of Havana
Partitioning Cuba into eastern and western occupation zones
Transferring Soviet missiles from Cuba to West Berlin

explanation: Khrushchev withdrew missiles from Cuba in return for a U.S. non-invasion pledge and U.S. Jupiter missile removal from Turkey.
fun_fact: After the crisis, Washington and Moscow installed a direct 'hotline' teletype link to prevent miscalculation.

trap_notes.b: President Kennedy chose a naval quarantine rather than an invasion.
trap_notes.c: Cuba remained under Fidel Castro's government without partition.
trap_notes.d: The missiles were shipped back to the Soviet Union, not West Berlin.
trap_notes.default: Quiet concessions on both Cuba and Turkey ended the nuclear standoff.

prompt: What environmental and economic trade-off accompanied the Green Revolution?

options.text: Higher grain yields required heavy irrigation and chemical fertilizers
New hybrid seeds eliminated all need for water or farm credit
Crop yields fell sharply in both Mexico and South Asia
Smallholder farmers stopped using machinery and fertilizers

explanation: Dwarf wheat and rice prevented famines, but depended on costly fertilizers, pesticides, and groundwater.
fun_fact: High-yield varieties often favored wealthier farmers who could afford tube wells and fertilizer.

trap_notes.b: High-yield crops actually needed more water and fertilizer than traditional varieties.
trap_notes.c: Grain harvests rose dramatically in Mexico, India, and Southeast Asia.
trap_notes.d: Green Revolution farming increased use of synthetic fertilizers and pumps.
trap_notes.default: Famine prevention came alongside heavy water and chemical demands.

prompt: How did domestic resistance and international pressure combine to end South African apartheid?

options.text: Mass strikes, ANC organizing, and global divestment forced negotiations
United Nations troops invaded Pretoria in 1960
Apartheid ended voluntarily before Nelson Mandela was imprisoned
Neighboring colonies annexed South Africa in 1990

explanation: Township protests, labor strikes, and international economic sanctions led to Mandela's release and 1994 elections.
fun_fact: Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison before becoming South Africa's first Black president in 1994.

trap_notes.b: No UN military invasion occurred; pressure came through sanctions and boycotts.
trap_notes.c: Apartheid lasted until the early 1990s, long after Mandela's 1962 arrest.
trap_notes.d: South Africa transitioned internally to multiracial democracy in 1994.
trap_notes.default: Internal resistance plus global economic sanctions brought the regime to negotiate.

prompt: What core goal drove France and West Germany to link their coal and steel industries in 1951?

options.text: Shared markets to make another war unthinkable
Closing European borders to transatlantic trade
Joining the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact trade bloc
Replacing modern factories with craft guilds

explanation: Pooling coal and steel—the raw materials of war—laid the foundation for the European Union.
fun_fact: The 1951 European Coal and Steel Community grew into the 1957 Common Market and 1993 European Union.

trap_notes.b: Western Europe remained closely tied to transatlantic trade.
trap_notes.c: France and West Germany were Western allies, not Warsaw Pact members.
trap_notes.d: The pact aimed to modernize heavy industry, not return to guilds.
trap_notes.default: Economic interdependence in coal and steel was designed to lock in peace.

prompt: How did Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika accelerate the Soviet Union's dissolution?

options.text: Openness unleashed nationalist movements while economic reforms disrupted central planning
Censorship tightened so strictly that Eastern Europe kept Communist rule
Soviet troops crushed every 1989 protest in Poland and East Germany
Perestroika instantly turned the USSR into the world's largest exporter

explanation: Political openness exposed past abuses and fueled republic independence, while partial reforms deepened shortages.
fun_fact: Gorbachev refused to send Soviet tanks to prop up Eastern European regimes in 1989.

trap_notes.b: Glasnost relaxed censorship, and Communist governments fell across Eastern Europe in 1989.
trap_notes.c: Unlike 1956 or 1968, Moscow did not use force to stop the 1989 revolutions.
trap_notes.d: The Soviet economy suffered severe shortages and output drops in 1989–1991.
trap_notes.default: Political openness plus disrupted central planning weakened Moscow's hold.

prompt: What caused the dramatic shrinking of Central Asia's Aral Sea after 1960?

options.text: Soviet planners diverted its feeder rivers to irrigate vast cotton fields
Melting Himalayan glaciers flooded the basin and broke its dams
Nuclear testing drained the sea into the Indian Ocean
Tectonic earthquakes lifted the seabed above sea level

explanation: Diverting the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers for Uzbek cotton starved the Aral Sea of inflow.
fun_fact: Fishing boats were left stranded miles from water on salt-crusted desert flats.

trap_notes.b: Excessive water diversion, not flooding, shrank the Aral Sea.
trap_notes.c: The Aral Sea is an endorheic basin with no outlet to the Indian Ocean.
trap_notes.d: Human irrigation canals, not earthquakes, caused the sea to dry up.
trap_notes.default: Diverting two major rivers for cotton irrigation dried up the Aral Sea.

prompt: How did standardized shipping containers transform late-20th-century manufacturing?

options.text: Slashing port loading costs let firms split production across global supply chains
Containers forced factories to stay next to coal mines inside Europe
Air freight replaced ocean shipping for heavy bulk goods
Ports needed more manual dockworkers to unpack every crate

explanation: Intermodal containers moved seamlessly from ship to rail to truck, slashing freight costs worldwide.
fun_fact: Standard 20- and 40-foot boxes cut ocean freight loading costs by more than 90 percent.

trap_notes.b: Cheap ocean shipping encouraged firms to locate factories wherever labor and inputs were cheapest.
trap_notes.c: Over 80% of world merchandise volume still travels by sea.
trap_notes.d: Cranes and standardized boxes dramatically reduced manual dock labor.
trap_notes.default: Lower transport costs made globalized manufacturing chains economical.

prompt: What common grievances sparked the 2010–2011 Arab Spring protests across North Africa and the Middle East?

options.text: Authoritarian corruption, youth unemployment, and rising food prices
Demands to restore Ottoman rule from Istanbul
Disputes over European Union eurozone membership
Protests against Cold War Soviet missile bases

explanation: Economic hardship, corruption, and lack of political freedom drove mass protests amplified by social media.
fun_fact: Protests began in Tunisia in December 2010 and quickly spread to Egypt, Libya, Yemen, and Syria.

trap_notes.b: The Ottoman Empire dissolved in 1922.
trap_notes.c: Arab Spring countries are not members of the European Union.
trap_notes.d: The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, twenty years earlier.
trap_notes.default: Economic frustration and authoritarian rule drove the 2010–2011 uprisings.

prompt: How did Alexander the Great's conquests reshape culture from Egypt to Central Asia?

options.text: Greek-speaking cities blended Hellenic art and science with Persian, Egyptian, and Indian traditions
Alexander banned all Greek language and philosophy outside Athens
Conquered regions adopted Latin as their sole administrative language
Trade between the Mediterranean and India stopped for three centuries

explanation: Hellenistic kingdoms fused Greek urban culture with local traditions, even influencing Gandharan Buddhist art.
fun_fact: Alexandria's Great Library attracted scholars like Euclid and Eratosthenes from across the Mediterranean.

trap_notes.b: Greek became the common scholarly and administrative language of the Hellenistic world.
trap_notes.c: Latin spread later with the Roman Empire, not Alexander's Greek kingdoms.
trap_notes.d: Hellenistic routes expanded trade linking the Mediterranean, Persia, and India.
trap_notes.default: Hellenistic culture blended Greek and local Afro-Eurasian traditions.

subdomain: Code of Hammurabi & Rule of Law
prompt: How did Hammurabi's Code differ from modern constitutional equality under the law?

options.text: Hammurabi's penalties varied sharply by social class, gender, and free or enslaved status
Hammurabi guaranteed identical fines for nobles and enslaved people
Babylonian judges were elected by universal adult suffrage
Hammurabi's laws were unwritten oral customs kept secret from citizens

explanation: While Hammurabi posted written laws publicly, punishments depended on whether a victim was elite, commoner, or enslaved.
fun_fact: Hammurabi's stele was carved in Akkadian cuneiform and displayed in public temple squares.

trap_notes.b: The code imposed harsher physical penalties on commoners and enslaved people than on elites.
trap_notes.c: Babylon was a hereditary monarchy, not a voting democracy.
trap_notes.d: Hammurabi famously inscribed his laws publicly on stone steles.
trap_notes.default: Written law existed in Babylon, but equal treatment across classes did not.

prompt: How did Little Ice Age cooling contribute to 17th-century political crises across Eurasia?

options.text: Crop failures triggered famines, tax revolts, and state strain
Warming seas melted polar ice and flooded Beijing and Paris
Abundant harvests ended peasant rebellions across Eurasia
Glaciers blocked Atlantic shipping between Spain and London

explanation: Colder winters and erratic rains reduced harvests, fueling peasant uprisings from Ming China to Europe.
fun_fact: Londoners occasionally held 'frost fairs' on the frozen River Thames during the coldest winters.

trap_notes.b: The Little Ice Age was a period of cooling, not global sea-level rise.
trap_notes.c: Harvest failures worsened hunger and helped topple the Ming Dynasty in 1644.
trap_notes.d: North Atlantic shipping routes remained open despite colder European winters.
trap_notes.default: Colder climates hurt harvests, raising food prices and social unrest.

prompt: How did colonized leaders in Asia and Africa respond to Woodrow Wilson's 1918 call for self-determination?

options.text: Many petitioned Versailles, then organized when denied
Britain and France immediately freed all colonies in 1919
Ho Chi Minh endorsed permanent French rule in Indochina
The League of Nations dissolved European empires in 1920

explanation: When Paris Peace talks denied colonial self-rule, activists like Ho Chi Minh turned toward anticolonial organizing.
fun_fact: In 1919, a young Ho Chi Minh worked in Paris and tried to hand a petition for Vietnamese rights to Wilson.

trap_notes.b: Britain and France actually expanded their holdings through League of Nations mandates.
trap_notes.c: Ho Chi Minh sought Vietnamese independence from French colonial rule.
trap_notes.d: The League mandate system preserved European oversight over former Ottoman and German territories.
trap_notes.default: Unfulfilled promises of self-determination in 1919 fueled anticolonial nationalism.

prompt: What pattern does the historical demographic transition model describe as societies industrialize and urbanize?

options.text: Death rates fall first, followed later by falling birth rates
Birth rates drop before clean water or vaccines arrive
Death rates rise sharply as cities add sewers and clinics
Urbanization tends to increase average family size

explanation: Cleaner water and medicine cut mortality first, causing rapid population growth until birth rates also decline.
fun_fact: Japan completed this transition rapidly after 1945 and now faces a shrinking, aging population.

trap_notes.b: Mortality declines first; fertility declines later as education and urban costs rise.
trap_notes.c: Sanitation and hospitals lower death rates rather than raising them.
trap_notes.d: Urban industrial economies typically see smaller family sizes over time.
trap_notes.default: Falling death rates precede falling birth rates, creating a surge in between.
